definition: Mist or fog, especially the cold haze that gathers in winter or at the foot of hills.
exampleSentence: By dawn a soft brume had settled over the valley, blurring the hedgerows into ghosts.
etymology: Borrowed from French brume, from Latin bruma, a contraction of brevissima dies, 'the shortest day' — so the word literally carries midwinter inside it. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Twilight; the soft half-light of dusk.
exampleSentence: In the gloam the garden lost its colours one by one until only the white roses remained.
etymology: A poetic back-formation related to the more common 'gloaming', from Old English glōm, 'twilight'. Merriam-Webster labels it archaic. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The beginning of evening; the falling of dusk.
exampleSentence: At evenfall the swallows came low over the water, stitching the last light to the dark.
etymology: A gentle Old English compound of 'even' (evening) and 'fall', recorded for centuries in pastoral verse. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Evening twilight; the hour at dusk.
exampleSentence: They walked home at cockshut, when the last rooks were folding into the elms.
etymology: From the time of day when poultry are shut in to roost; first recorded in 1592 and used by Shakespeare in Richard III ('Much about cockshut time, from troop to troop'). Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The dim light of dusk or early evening, when owls begin to stir.
exampleSentence: We lingered in the owl-light until the hills became one shadow and the first call drifted across the field.
etymology: A charming compound of 'owl' and 'light', recorded since the 1500s for the half-light favoured by owls. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The first light of day; the dawn, often with a sense of new beginning.
exampleSentence: At the dayspring the frost on the meadow flared pink, and the whole field seemed to draw breath.
etymology: A 14th-century compound meaning the 'springing up' of day, made famous by its appearance in the Gospel of Luke. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The forming of dew, and the hour of evening when it begins to settle.
exampleSentence: By dewfall the grass had turned silver and cold, and our footprints darkened behind us.
etymology: A quiet English compound of 'dew' and 'fall', recorded since the 19th century for both the moisture and the moment. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The glow that lingers in the sky after sunset; also the warm feeling that remains after a happy experience.
exampleSentence: Long after the others had gone to bed she sat in the afterglow of the day, unwilling to let it end.
etymology: A 19th-century compound of 'after' and 'glow' that drifted naturally from the sky into the heart. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A rainbow formed by moonlight rather than sun, faint and often ghostly pale.
exampleSentence: Above the waterfall a moonbow hung in the spray, so faint we doubted our own eyes.
etymology: A modern compound of 'moon' and 'bow', describing a phenomenon noted as far back as Aristotle. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The eerie phosphorescent glow given off by certain fungi on rotting wood.
exampleSentence: Deep in the wood the fallen logs gave off a faint foxfire, a cold green light with no flame at all.
etymology: Possibly from Old French fois ('false'), so 'false fire'; an old country name for the glow of luminous fungi. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Fine filmy cobweb seen floating in calm air; anything exquisitely light and delicate.
exampleSentence: Threads of gossamer drifted across the lane, catching the low sun like spun glass.
etymology: From Middle English 'goose summer' — the mild late-autumn spell when such webs appear, perhaps because the silk resembled goose down. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: (Of wind) blowing strongly with a roaring sound; (of a place) exposed to such wind.
exampleSentence: The farmhouse stood on a wuthering ridge where the wind never quite stopped its low complaint.
etymology: A Yorkshire dialect word from Old Norse hvitha, 'a squall of wind', made immortal by Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The vault of the heavens; the sky regarded as a great arching expanse.
exampleSentence: Out where no town lights reached, the whole firmament blazed at once and we forgot to speak.
etymology: From Latin firmamentum, 'a support', via the Vulgate's rendering of the sky as a solid dome. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The highest reaches of heaven; the realm of pure light and fire.
exampleSentence: From the summit the dawn seemed to open straight into the empyrean, gold upon endless gold.
etymology: From Greek empyros, 'fiery', the ancients' name for the heaven of pure flame beyond the stars; used by Milton and Dante. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Deep sky-blue; the clear blue of a cloudless heaven or calm sea.
exampleSentence: The lake lay perfectly cerulean, a single colour from shore to shore.
etymology: From Latin caeruleus, 'dark blue', related to caelum, 'sky' — so the colour is named for heaven itself. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A swelling, rounded mass of cumulus cloud rising before a thunderstorm.
exampleSentence: A thunderhead stacked itself over the plain all afternoon, white at the top and bruised below.
etymology: A vivid American compound of 'thunder' and 'head', for the towering head of a storm cloud. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sky dappled with rows of small white clouds resembling the markings on a mackerel's back.
exampleSentence: A mackerel sky spread overhead at evening, ribbed and silver, promising a change in the weather.
etymology: A sailors' and shepherds' phrase, recorded for centuries in the rhyme 'mackerel sky, never long wet, never long dry'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fertile, low-lying coastal grassland of the Scottish and Irish west, famous for its summer carpet of wildflowers.
exampleSentence: In June the machair erupts into a riot of orchids and clover above the white sand.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic machair, 'fertile plain'; one of the rarest habitats in Europe, found only on the windward Atlantic shores. Listed in Collins.

definition: A small rocky island or reef, often awash at high tide.
exampleSentence: Seals hauled out on the skerry at low water, grey humps on the black rock.
etymology: From Old Norse sker via the Scots of Orkney and Shetland, where such rocks fringe every coast. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small bay or narrow sea inlet, as found in Orkney and Shetland.
exampleSentence: The boat slipped into the still voe, where the only sound was water lapping on shingle.
etymology: From Old Norse vágr, 'bay'; a Northern Isles word for the long fingers of sea that reach into the land. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A waterfall, or the deep pool at its foot; also a steep ravine.
exampleSentence: We followed the burn until it tumbled white over the linn into a pool black with peat.
etymology: A Scots word, recorded from 1513, blending Scottish Gaelic linne ('pool') with Old English hlynn ('torrent'). Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A sudden rise or rush of a stream from heavy rain or melting snow; a small freshwater rivulet.
exampleSentence: The spring freshet came down off the mountain overnight and turned the quiet brook into a roar.
etymology: From 'fresh' plus the diminutive -et; in use since the 1500s for the swelling of streams in thaw. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A sudden flood in a river; by extension, a rush or outpouring of anything.
exampleSentence: After three days of rain the river was in spate, brown and muscular between its banks.
etymology: A word of Scots and northern English origin, of uncertain root, long used for rivers running high. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A circular movement of water, air or mist running contrary to the main current.
exampleSentence: Leaves spun in a slow eddy at the river's edge, going nowhere, content to circle.
etymology: Probably from Old Norse iða, 'whirlpool'; in English since the 15th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small stream or trickling brook.
exampleSentence: A thread-thin rill ran down the hillside, singing to itself among the stones.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Low German or Dutch ril; a favourite of poets from Milton onward. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A tiny stream or rivulet; a little channel of running water.
exampleSentence: Rain gathered into a runnel along the gutter and carried a fleet of petals away.
etymology: An alteration of the older 'rinel', from Old English rynel, a diminutive of 'run'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A brook or mountain stream, especially one with a stony bed (Northern English).
exampleSentence: The children spent the whole afternoon damming the beck with pebbles and shrieking at the cold.
etymology: From Old Norse bekkr, 'brook'; the ordinary word for a stream across much of northern England. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small steep-banked mountain lake or pool.
exampleSentence: High above the valley a black tarn lay perfectly still, mirroring a sky it would never reach.
etymology: From Old Norse tjǫrn, 'small mountain lake'; a word native to the fells of northern England. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A lake, pool or broad expanse of standing water (poetic and dialectal).
exampleSentence: Mist hung low over the mere at dawn, so that the reeds seemed to grow out of cloud.
etymology: From Old English mere, 'sea, lake'; the OED marks the lake sense as poetical or dialectal. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A small, deep, wooded valley or dell.
exampleSentence: Bluebells flooded the dingle so thickly that the floor of the wood looked like spilled sky.
etymology: From Middle English meaning 'a deep hollow', perhaps akin to Old English dung. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A short, deep valley running into a hillside, often dry at the head.
exampleSentence: They followed the lane into a quiet combe where sheep grazed and the wind could not reach.
etymology: From Old English cumb, ultimately of Celtic origin; common in West Country place names. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A steep, bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a valley, carved by ice.
exampleSentence: Snow lingered in the high cwm long after the lower slopes had turned to green.
etymology: Borrowed directly from Welsh cwm, 'valley'; one of the few English words with no vowel letter. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A rounded hollow scooped into a mountainside by a former glacier.
exampleSentence: We ate our lunch in the shelter of the corrie, ringed by cliffs and the cries of ravens.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic coire, 'cauldron'; the Highland name for these natural mountain amphitheatres. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge, usually with a stream running through it.
exampleSentence: The path dropped into a shadowed clough where ferns dripped and the beck rang on the rocks.
etymology: From Old English clōh; a dialect word of the Pennines for a wooded cleft in the hills. Listed in Collins.

definition: A narrow, secluded valley, especially among mountains.
exampleSentence: Smoke rose straight from a single chimney far down the glen, the only sign of anyone at all.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic and Irish gleann, 'valley'; carried into English from the Celtic north and west. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A valley, especially a wide and gentle one (chiefly poetic).
exampleSentence: Below them lay a green vale threaded by a river, almost too peaceful to be real.
etymology: From Old French val, from Latin vallis, 'valley'; long beloved of poets for its softness of sound. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: An open meadow or grassland, especially one used for grazing.
exampleSentence: At dusk the cattle moved slowly across the lea, dark shapes against the failing gold.
etymology: From Old English lēah, 'open ground, clearing'; one of the oldest words in the English landscape. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A tract of open, rolling upland or down.
exampleSentence: The road ran for miles across the bare wold, with nothing between us and the sky.
etymology: From Old English weald, 'forest, high open land'; the same root as 'weald'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A high, barren hill or stretch of moorland (Northern English).
exampleSentence: They climbed the fell in a clinging mist and broke through, suddenly, into clean cold sunlight.
etymology: From Old Norse fjall, 'mountain'; the everyday word for the high ground of Cumbria and the north. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A hillside or the steep bank of a river or valley (Scots).
exampleSentence: She ran down the brae with her arms wide, the wind taking her laughter up the glen.
etymology: From Old Norse brá, 'eyelash, brow', via Scots, where it names every slope in the land. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A high, weathered outcrop of rock crowning a hill, especially on moorland.
exampleSentence: The granite tor stood against the sky like the ruin of some forgotten tower.
etymology: From Old English torr, of Celtic origin; characteristic of Dartmoor and the West Country. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small wood or wooded hill (archaic and poetic).
exampleSentence: At the edge of the holt a single deer lifted its head, then was gone among the trees.
etymology: From Old English holt, 'wood'; Merriam-Webster and Collins mark this sense archaic or poetic. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small wood or thicket, especially one planted to shelter game.
exampleSentence: A blackcap was singing somewhere in the little spinney behind the barn.
etymology: From Old French espinei, 'a thorny place', from Latin spina, 'thorn'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A pleasant shady recess in a garden or wood, sheltered by leaves and boughs.
exampleSentence: They found a green bower of hazel where the light fell in coins and no one could see them.
etymology: From Old English būr, 'dwelling, chamber'; later the leafy retreat of pastoral poetry. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A light, springing rhythm in music or speech; a gentle rise and fall.
exampleSentence: There was a lilt in her voice when she spoke of home that she never seemed to notice.
etymology: From Middle English lilten, of obscure origin, first used of merry singing. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A low, continuous humming or vibrating sound.
exampleSentence: All night the thrum of rain on the tin roof held us somewhere between sleep and waking.
etymology: Imitative in origin, echoing the sound it names; in English since the 16th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To make a bubbling, gurgling sound, as flowing water does.
exampleSentence: The stream burbled over its stones in the dark, a sound so steady it felt like company.
etymology: Imitative, formed in Middle English to mimic the noise of bubbling water. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To sing with trills and quavering, sweet notes, as a bird does.
exampleSentence: A blackbird warbled from the topmost twig as though daring the morning to stay grey.
etymology: From Old French werbler, 'to sing with trills', of Germanic origin. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A temporary calm or quiet, especially a pause in a storm or in activity.
exampleSentence: In the lull between songs you could hear the sea, patient and enormous, beyond the open door.
etymology: Imitative, from the soothing sounds used to quiet a child to sleep (compare 'lullaby'). Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The slow, solemn sound of a bell, especially one rung for a death or ending.
exampleSentence: The single knell carried over the rooftops, and for a moment the whole town seemed to pause.
etymology: From Old English cnyllan, 'to strike a bell'; long associated with mourning. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A slow, mournful song or lament for the dead.
exampleSentence: The wind in the chimney kept up its low dirge while the house slept on around it.
etymology: From Latin dirige, 'direct', the first word of a Latin funeral antiphon. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To wail in grief; to lament loudly for the dead in the Irish tradition.
exampleSentence: The women keened at the graveside, a sound older than any words could be.
etymology: From Irish caoinim, 'I weep'; the keening of mourners is an ancient funeral rite. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fragrant essential oil distilled from flowers, especially rose petals.
exampleSentence: One drop of attar of roses filled the whole room, summoning a summer years gone by.
etymology: From Persian and Arabic ʿitr, 'perfume, essence'; the costliest of rose distillations. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A gentle current of scent, sound or air drifting by.
exampleSentence: A waft of woodsmoke reached her on the path, and at once she was eight years old again.
etymology: From the verb 'waft', probably from Dutch or Low German wachten, 'to guard, escort'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Something fragrant and soothing; anything that heals, comforts or eases pain.
exampleSentence: After the noise of the city, the silence of the hills was pure balm.
etymology: From Latin balsamum, 'aromatic resin'; the soothing of the body became the soothing of the soul. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fit of low spirits or sulky gloom; a vague, causeless melancholy.
exampleSentence: A grey Sunday always gives me the mulligrubs, that low gloom with no real cause behind it.
etymology: A fanciful 16th-century coinage, perhaps from 'megrim'; once also meant a stomach gripe. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A fit of low spirits or depression; also a passing whim or fancy.
exampleSentence: He shut the curtains, took to his chair, and gave himself up to the megrims for the afternoon.
etymology: An old form of 'migraine', from Greek hēmikrania, 'half the skull'; the headache became a mood and a caprice. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A weary listlessness and dissatisfaction born of boredom and a sense of life's emptiness.
exampleSentence: By the third week of rain a great ennui had settled over the house, heavier than any task.
etymology: From French ennui, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred'; long naturalised in English. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A pleasant or dreamy weariness; a soft, heavy lack of energy.
exampleSentence: A warm languor stole over them on the riverbank, and no one could be bothered to row home.
etymology: From Latin languere, 'to be faint or weak'; in English the word softened into something almost luxurious. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A state of weary listlessness; physical or mental fatigue and lack of will.
exampleSentence: A heavy lassitude held her to the bed, as though the air itself had grown too thick to move through.
etymology: From Latin lassus, 'weary'; the noun of pure tiredness. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A spell of low spirits, listlessness or stagnation; a period when nothing seems to move.
exampleSentence: January found him in the doldrums, the holidays gone and spring still impossibly far off.
etymology: From 'dull', influenced by 'tantrum'; later the name for the calm equatorial belt where sailing ships stalled. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Restlessness or uneasiness of mind; a quiet, nagging disquiet.
exampleSentence: A faint inquietude kept her at the window long after midnight, watching a road where no one came.
etymology: From Latin inquietudo, 'unrest', from in- ('not') plus quietus ('calm'). Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Tearfully or weakly sentimental, often after drink or in self-pity.
exampleSentence: Two glasses of wine and he turned maudlin, dredging up every old sorrow he could find.
etymology: From the name Mary Magdalene, often depicted weeping; her name softened into a word for tears. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Tearful; given to weeping, or tending to bring tears.
exampleSentence: The film was so relentlessly lachrymose that by the end the whole row was sniffling into their sleeves.
etymology: From Latin lacrima, 'tear'; a word that almost weeps as you say it. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Expressing or sounding a wistful sorrow; mournful in a soft, appealing way.
exampleSentence: A plaintive whistle came from the marsh, the loneliest sound she had ever heard.
etymology: From Old French plaintif, from plainte, 'lament'; the same root as 'complain'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Feeling or showing gentle, wry regret or sorrow.
exampleSentence: She gave a rueful smile at the photograph, half-amused, half-mournful at who they used to be.
etymology: From Old English hrēow, 'sorrow, repentance'; the same root as 'rue', the herb of regret. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To feel or express discontent; to fret or pine in low spirits.
exampleSentence: There was no use to repine over the lost letters; she packed them away and turned to the window.
etymology: Formed from 're-' plus 'pine', 'to languish with longing'; in use since the 1500s. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To be overcome with rapture or emotion, almost to the point of fainting.
exampleSentence: The first warm evening of the year, with lilac on the air, was enough to make anyone swoon.
etymology: From Old English geswōgen, 'in a faint'; later the word for being undone by feeling. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Hopelessly infatuated; so smitten as to lose all sense.
exampleSentence: He was utterly besotted, walking into lampposts because he could not stop reading her letters.
etymology: From 'be-' plus 'sot', 'fool'; literally to be made foolish, here by love. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Pining from unrequited or lost love; forsaken by the one you love.
exampleSentence: He wandered the lovelorn weeks of autumn writing letters he would never send.
etymology: From 'love' plus 'lorn', an old past participle of 'leese', 'to lose'; literally 'lost in love'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Looking sorrowful, dejected or in a sorry state.
exampleSentence: He sat on the kerb, woebegone, clutching the ticket for the train he had just missed.
etymology: From Middle English wo begon, 'beset with woe'; the woe has, quite literally, gone all over you. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Grieved or sorrowful at heart; aching with sadness.
exampleSentence: She left the old house heartsore, looking back once at the window of her childhood room.
etymology: A plain, old English compound of 'heart' and 'sore'; the soreness is grief itself. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Full of sadness; melancholy and pensive.
exampleSentence: There was something tristful in the way the light left the room, slow and reluctant as a goodbye.
etymology: From Latin tristis, 'sad', via Old French; a quieter cousin of 'sad' that English has nearly forgotten. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: So unhappy that nothing can console or comfort you.
exampleSentence: The dog lay disconsolate by the door for days after the boy went away to school.
etymology: From Latin disconsolatus, 'without solace', from consolari, 'to comfort'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Deprived of something or someone dear, and left desolate by the loss.
exampleSentence: With the last guest gone and the lights off, the house felt suddenly bereft.
etymology: The old past participle of 'bereave', from Old English berēafian, 'to rob, deprive'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Dejected and dispirited, with one's pride or hopes suddenly cast down.
exampleSentence: He came back from the audition crestfallen, his sheet music still rolled tight in his fist.
etymology: From the drooping crest of a defeated cockerel; the metaphor dates from the 1500s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A faint or desperate hope that is very unlikely to be fulfilled.
exampleSentence: He kept the porch light burning every night, a forlorn hope that she might still find her way back.
synonyms: vain hope, long shot, desperate venture
etymology: A mishearing of Dutch verloren hoop, 'lost troop' — once a band of soldiers sent on a doomed first assault, now a hope against hope. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Deep, sincere sorrow and remorse for having done wrong.
exampleSentence: His contrition was real; you could see it in the way he could not meet anyone's eyes.
etymology: From Latin contritus, 'worn down, crushed'; sorrow that grinds the heart small. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Engaged in deep, dreamy and often slightly sad thought.
exampleSentence: She grew pensive at the station, watching the rails run together toward a place she would not go.
etymology: From Old French pensif, from penser, 'to think', from Latin pensare, 'to weigh'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Full of gentle, yearning sadness; longing for something lost or unattainable.
exampleSentence: He gave a wistful glance at the children playing, remembering when summers had no end.
etymology: Probably from the older 'wistly', 'intently', blended with 'wishful'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Giving or showing joy; cheerful and full of gladness.
exampleSentence: A gladsome noise of children spilled out of the schoolyard and filled the whole grey street.
etymology: From Old English glæd, 'glad', plus '-some'; a word that has kept its old warmth. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Cheerful, merry and lighthearted.
exampleSentence: She set off down the lane in a blithesome mood, swinging her basket and humming to no one.
etymology: From Old English blīthe, 'happy, kindly', plus '-some'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Nimble and graceful; also cheerful and free from care.
exampleSentence: With the exams behind her she felt suddenly lightsome, as if she might float up the stairs.
etymology: From 'light' plus '-some'; meaning both 'full of light' and 'light of heart'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Cheerful and lighthearted; sprightly with good humour.
exampleSentence: The whole company grew jocund as the fire took hold and the songs began.
etymology: From Latin jucundus, 'pleasant', influenced by jocus, 'joke'; used by Wordsworth of his dancing daffodils. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Overflowing with excitement, enthusiasm and high spirits.
exampleSentence: She was ebullient after the good news, unable to sit still or stop talking for an hour.
etymology: From Latin ebullire, 'to boil over'; high spirits literally bubbling up. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Full of eager anticipation and excitement.
exampleSentence: The children were agog at the window, breath fogging the glass, waiting for the first snow.
etymology: Probably from Old French en gogues, 'in merriment'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A state of awed astonishment and curious delight.
exampleSentence: She gazed up into the cathedral's vaulting in pure wonderment, her argument quite forgotten.
etymology: From 'wonder' plus '-ment'; in English since the 16th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Extravagantly enthusiastic or ecstatic; overflowing with joyful feeling.
exampleSentence: He went rhapsodic about the little harbour town, as if no one had ever seen the sea before.
etymology: From Greek rhapsōidia, the recitation of epic poetry; later any flight of ardent feeling. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A state of supreme blessedness, serene and complete happiness.
exampleSentence: For one whole afternoon, with the baby asleep on her chest, she knew a kind of beatitude.
etymology: From Latin beatus, 'blessed, happy'; the same root as the Beatitudes of the Gospels. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Calmness and composure, especially under strain; an even, untroubled mind.
exampleSentence: She bore the long delay with an equanimity the rest of us could only envy.
etymology: From Latin aequus animus, 'even mind'; the balance of a steady spirit. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Delight and enjoyment; the pleasure taken in something agreeable.
exampleSentence: He laid out the cheeses and the wine with evident delectation, rubbing his hands together.
etymology: From Latin delectatio, 'a delighting', from delectare, 'to charm'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A deep, cosy contentment created by simple comforts, warmth and good company.
exampleSentence: Candles lit, wool socks on, the storm shut outside and the kettle singing — that is hygge.
etymology: A Danish untranslatable, from a Norwegian word for 'wellbeing'; Collins named it a Word of the Year in 2016. A foreign untranslatable from Danish. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Odds and ends; assorted small objects or bits and pieces, often of little value.
exampleSentence: He emptied his pockets onto the table: keys, string, a conker, and all the usual gubbins.
synonyms: odds and ends, bits and pieces, paraphernalia, clutter
etymology: From the old word 'gobbon', 'a fragment'; Merriam-Webster labels it British dialect. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fanciful ornament or contrivance; a trinket, knick-knack or whim.
exampleSentence: The mantelpiece was crowded with whigmaleeries — tiny brass animals, a glass dome, a clock that never told the truth.
etymology: A playful 18th-century Scots word of unknown origin; Merriam-Webster and Collins both mark it chiefly Scottish. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Something full of twists and turns; fanciful, excessively intricate detail.
exampleSentence: The old map was a crinkum-crankum of lanes and footpaths that led, as far as we could tell, nowhere.
etymology: A reduplication of 'crank', 'a bend or twist'; first recorded in the 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A confused jumble or hotchpotch of unrelated things.
exampleSentence: Her desk was a gallimaufry of receipts, seashells and half-finished poems.
etymology: From 16th-century French galimafrée, a stew thrown together from odd scraps of meat. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A confused mixture or hodgepodge, especially of ideas or nonsense.
exampleSentence: The pamphlet was a farrago of rumour, half-truth and pure invention, and he believed every word.
etymology: From Latin farrago, 'mixed fodder for cattle', from far, 'grain'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A noisy and overexcited reaction; a hubbub or fuss.
exampleSentence: There was a tremendous brouhaha at the gate, all of it over a goat that had escaped its pen.
etymology: From French brouhaha, probably imitative of confused noise. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A commotion or fuss, especially one caused by disagreement.
exampleSentence: There was a great kerfuffle over the seating plan, and in the end nobody sat where they were told.
etymology: From Scots curfuffle, from Gaelic car, 'to twist', plus fuffle, 'to dishevel'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A brief but deeply unpleasant or embarrassing experience.
exampleSentence: Waiting outside the head teacher's office, he lived through a genuine mauvais quart d'heure.
etymology: A French phrase, literally 'bad quarter of an hour', naturalised into English. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.
